quran.note: Yusuf tells his father of eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to him; Ya’qub tells him not to tell his brothers.
The brothers say their father is in clear error and plot against Yusuf; “a speaker among them” says do not kill him but throw him into the well.
They ask to take him out to play, put him in the well, and come at night weeping with false blood on his shirt; Ya’qub says patience is most fitting.
A caravan finds him; he is sold for a reduced price, a few dirhams.
The wife of the man he lived with tries to seduce him; he says “[I seek] the refuge of Allah”; the shirt torn from behind shows who is in the wrong.
The women of the city talk; the women who cut their hands; Yusuf’s prayer, “prison is more to my liking”; they decide to imprison him.
In prison he interprets the dreams of two young men and calls them to Allah alone.
The king’s dream of seven fat cows and seven lean, and Yusuf’s interpretation and plan.
Yusuf asks that the matter of the women be investigated; the wife of the Aziz says the truth has become evident; “I do not acquit myself.”
Yusuf is made trustworthy in the king’s service and asks to be put over the storehouses of the land.
The cup in his brother’s bag, “Thus did We plan for Yusuf.”
Ya’qub’s grief, “I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah”; he tells his sons to go and find out about Yusuf.
The shirt over his father’s face; the family comes to Egypt; his dream is fulfilled.
Yusuf’s prayer: “Cause me to die a Muslim and join me with the righteous.”

hadith.summary: Asked who was the most honoured of people with Allah, the Prophet ﷺ said the most righteous. When they said that was not what they meant, he said Yusuf, a prophet of Allah, the son of a prophet, the son of a prophet, the son of the khalil of Allah (Ibrahim). They said again that was not what they meant, and he spoke of the Arabs and said those who were best before Islam are best in Islam if they gain understanding of the religion.

The Prophet ﷺ said that if he had stayed in prison as long as Yusuf did, he would have answered the call to come out at once. The same report mentions his doubt-and-heart-at-ease remark about Ibrahim and his prayer for mercy on Lut; it is given in full under Ibrahim.

In the Prophet’s ﷺ account of the night journey, Yusuf is the prophet in the third heaven and the report says he had been given half of all beauty. The same report names Adam in the first heaven, Isa and Yahya in the second, Idris in the fourth, Harun in the fifth, Musa in the sixth and Ibrahim in the seventh.
In the Prophet’s ﷺ account of the night journey, Yusuf is the prophet in the third heaven; he welcomed the Prophet ﷺ as a brother and a prophet.

scholarly.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
scholarly.author: Ibn Kathir
scholarly.summary: Records Ibn Abbas that the dreams of prophets are revelation. It reads the eleven stars as Yusuf’s eleven brothers and the sun and moon as his father and mother, a reading attributed to Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Sufyan al-Thawri and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, and says the dream came true about forty years later, though some say eighty.

scholarly.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
scholarly.author: Ibn Kathir
scholarly.summary: On “had he not seen the proof of his Lord”: quotes Ibn Jarir al-Tabari that Yusuf saw a sign from Allah which turned away his desire, and that the three suggestions for what it was (the image of Ya’qub, an angel, or a divine command) have no clear proof, so the matter should be left as general as the Qur’an leaves it. The text also says it was “also reported” that he was about to strike her, naming no source and neither accepting nor rejecting it.

scholarly.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
scholarly.author: Ibn Kathir
scholarly.summary: Holds that “I do not acquit myself” is the speech of the wife of the Aziz, not of Yusuf, as the most fitting reading of the flow of the story: she continues what she said before the king, while Yusuf was not yet present, having been released and brought afterwards. It names al-Mawardi and Ibn Taymiyyah as holding this view.

scholarly.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
scholarly.author: Ibn Kathir
scholarly.summary: Records Qatadah and others that Ya’qub kept his sorrow to himself and complained to no one among creation, and a report through Sa’id ibn Jubayr that he lost his sight through the sorrow he held back. It gives Ibn Abbas that “I know from Allah what you do not know” refers to Yusuf’s vision being true and Allah bringing it to pass.

differences.question: Who says “I do not acquit myself” (12:53)?

views.who: Ibn Kathir, al-Mawardi and Ibn Taymiyyah
views.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
views.view: The wife of the Aziz, speaking before the king.

views.who: Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim
views.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com), on 12:53
views.view: Yusuf, speaking after he had sent back the king’s messenger so that the matter could be investigated.

differences.note: The abridged text calls the first reading “the most viable and suitable”.
